name: Mongolia

facts.religion: Tibetan Buddhism about 50%, no religion about 40%, shamanism

snapshot: A ruling-party feud forced Prime Minister Zandanshatar out in March 2026, Mongolia's latest change of government in a democracy squeezed between Russia and China.
culture: Genghis Khan is the founding hero of the nation. Around a quarter of Mongolians still live as herders, moving with their gers, felt tents, across the steppe. Naadam, the summer festival of wrestling, horse racing and archery, is the highlight of the year. Throat singing and the horsehead fiddle are UNESCO-listed.
society: Mongolia's economy depends on coal and copper exports to China, especially from the giant Oyu Tolgoi mine. Half the population lives in Ulaanbaatar, where winter air pollution is among the world's worst. Harsh winters called dzud kill millions of livestock. Corruption scandals regularly bring down governments.
situation: Mongolia is a democracy wedged between Russia and China, two of the world's most powerful authoritarian states, and it has stayed one since its peaceful revolution in 1990. That is a real achievement. But in 2026 the country showed how fragile a democracy can be when one party wins everything and then fights itself.

On 27 March, Prime Minister Gombojav Zandanshatar resigned after nine months in office, warning that "the world is entering a critical geopolitical period" (AFP via Citizen Digital). He had already survived one attempt by parliament to remove him, blocked by the Constitutional Court in October. The pressure came from corruption allegations against his justice minister, a boycott of parliament by the opposition Democratic Party, and above all a feud inside the ruling Mongolian People's Party between factions loyal to President Ukhnaa Khurelsukh and to former prime minister Oyun-Erdene, who had fallen in 2025. Parliament confirmed party chairman and speaker Uchral Nyam-Osor as Mongolia's third prime minister in about a year, seen as a compromise between the factions (AP via WTOP). Why it matters to ordinary Mongolians: the country lives on coal and copper sold to China and imports all its fuel, so the Iran war's oil shock hit hard, and every change of government means shifting mining rules that scare off the investment that pays for pensions and wages.
power: A semi-presidential democracy. The president is directly elected for a single six-year term and has veto and some security powers; the 126-seat State Great Khural elects the prime minister, who runs the government.
holders: Prime Minister Uchral Nyam-Osor (MPP); President Ukhnaa Khurelsukh.
